headline: Amber-lens bipolar paper is hypothesis-level virtual-darkness context.
implication: Do not cite as proof of bedtime glasses efficacy.
caveat: No empirical outcome data.

headline: Mania case report showed sleep regularity and symptom improvement after blue-light blocking.
implication: Historical clinical signal only; not consumer efficacy evidence.
caveat: Single case report with no comparator.

headline: Morning blue-blockers may help daytime sleep after permanent night shifts.
implication: Shows that eyewear timing is schedule-dependent; it is not direct bedtime evidence.
caveat: Permanent night-work context and pilot design.

headline: Blue-green night light plus daytime blue-blockers showed pilot shift-work adaptation signals.
implication: Keep shift-work adaptation separate from bedtime protocol claims.
caveat: Combined timed intervention in night workers.

headline: Supervised dark therapy accelerated improvement in a small mania pilot.
implication: Provides historical clinical rationale for virtual darkness, not standalone consumer sleep efficacy.
caveat: Acute psychiatric treatment setting with enforced darkness.

headline: MDD sleep-onset insomnia eyewear trial is a psychiatric boundary source, not direct protocol proof.
implication: Requires population-specific caveats before any claim transfer.
caveat: Effect estimates and safety details were not fully extracted from accessible metadata.

headline: Filtering short wavelengths during nocturnal shiftwork showed sleep/performance signals in a very small sample.
implication: Keeps shift-work eyewear findings separate from consumer bedtime claims.
caveat: Nine-participant shift-work study; not a red-glasses-before-bed trial.

headline: Actigraphy sleep parameters favored blue-blocking glasses in a mania-treatment context.
implication: Supports clinical boundary language and actigraphy endpoints, not consumer sleep claims.
caveat: Small inpatient secondary analysis.

headline: Amber lenses improved insomnia ratings and actigraphy total sleep time in adults with insomnia symptoms.
implication: Strong direct support for testing the protocol in symptomatic sleepers, especially with 2-hour pre-bed wear.
caveat: n=14 and 7-night condition periods; not all actigraphy metrics improved.

headline: Commercial blue-blocking glasses vary widely; color alone does not prove melanopic filtering strength.
implication: Supports a lens-quality guardrail based on spectral data, fit, edge leakage, timing, and surrounding light conditions.
caveat: Review and product characterization; not a new randomized home sleep trial.

headline: Practice Parameters for the Role of Actigraphy in the Study of Sleep and Circadian Rhythms: An Update for 2002 is measurement-context evidence for wearable/actigraphy endpoint interpretation.
implication: Use this source to frame sleep-onset, sleep-efficiency, WASO, duration, or sleep-stage outputs as noisy measurement signals; it does not support a direct efficacy claim for red-light glasses before bed.
caveat: Guideline/practice-parameter source rather than a validation trial of red-light glasses; recommendations depend on the evidence base available in 2002.

headline: The Role of Actigraphy in the Study of Sleep and Circadian Rhythms is measurement-context evidence for wearable/actigraphy endpoint interpretation.
implication: Use this source to frame sleep-onset, sleep-efficiency, WASO, duration, or sleep-stage outputs as noisy measurement signals; it does not support a direct efficacy claim for red-light glasses before bed.
caveat: Narrative review; device algorithms and validation standards have changed since 2003.

headline: Actigraphy in the Assessment of Insomnia is measurement-context evidence for wearable/actigraphy endpoint interpretation.
implication: Use this source to frame sleep-onset, sleep-efficiency, WASO, duration, or sleep-stage outputs as noisy measurement signals; it does not support a direct efficacy claim for red-light glasses before bed.
caveat: Not a red-light-glasses trial; older actigraphy methods may not match current consumer devices.

headline: Wake Detection Capacity of Actigraphy During Sleep is measurement-context evidence for wearable/actigraphy endpoint interpretation.
implication: Use this source to frame sleep-onset, sleep-efficiency, WASO, duration, or sleep-stage outputs as noisy measurement signals; it does not support a direct efficacy claim for red-light glasses before bed.
caveat: Small healthy-subject validation; not a red-light-glasses intervention and not a consumer-wearable study.

headline: Evaluation of Immobility Time for Sleep Latency in Actigraphy is measurement-context evidence for wearable/actigraphy endpoint interpretation.
implication: Use this source to frame sleep-onset, sleep-efficiency, WASO, duration, or sleep-stage outputs as noisy measurement signals; it does not support a direct efficacy claim for red-light glasses before bed.
caveat: Scoring-method source rather than efficacy evidence; immobility does not necessarily equal sleep.

headline: Measuring Sleep: Accuracy, Sensitivity, and Specificity of Wrist Actigraphy Compared to Polysomnography is measurement-context evidence for wearable/actigraphy endpoint interpretation.
implication: Use this source to frame sleep-onset, sleep-efficiency, WASO, duration, or sleep-stage outputs as noisy measurement signals; it does not support a direct efficacy claim for red-light glasses before bed.
caveat: Validation context rather than intervention evidence; PSG-lab conditions and actigraphy algorithms may not match a user’s current wearable.

headline: Use of Actigraphy for the Evaluation of Sleep Disorders and Circadian Rhythm Sleep-Wake Disorders: An American Academy of Sleep Medicine Clinical Practice Guideline is measurement-context evidence for wearable/actigraphy endpoint interpretation.
implication: Use this source to frame sleep-onset, sleep-efficiency, WASO, duration, or sleep-stage outputs as noisy measurement signals; it does not support a direct efficacy claim for red-light glasses before bed.
caveat: Guideline recommendations are indication-specific; actigraphy still does not replace full clinical diagnosis where PSG or clinical evaluation is needed.

headline: A Systematic Review of the Accuracy of Sleep Wearable Devices for Estimating Sleep Onset is measurement-context evidence for wearable/actigraphy endpoint interpretation.
implication: Use this source to frame sleep-onset, sleep-efficiency, WASO, duration, or sleep-stage outputs as noisy measurement signals; it does not support a direct efficacy claim for red-light glasses before bed.
caveat: Heterogeneous devices and algorithms; not direct intervention evidence for red-light glasses.

headline: Actigraphy-Based Assessment of Sleep Parameters is measurement-context evidence for wearable/actigraphy endpoint interpretation.
implication: Use this source to frame sleep-onset, sleep-efficiency, WASO, duration, or sleep-stage outputs as noisy measurement signals; it does not support a direct efficacy claim for red-light glasses before bed.
caveat: Methodology context; not a validation of red-light glasses or a consumer-device efficacy study.

headline: Performance of Seven Consumer Sleep-Tracking Devices Compared with Polysomnography is measurement-context evidence for wearable/actigraphy endpoint interpretation.
implication: Use this source to frame sleep-onset, sleep-efficiency, WASO, duration, or sleep-stage outputs as noisy measurement signals; it does not support a direct efficacy claim for red-light glasses before bed.
caveat: Healthy young-adult lab sample; devices and algorithms may not generalize to current models or clinical populations; not protocol efficacy evidence.

headline: State of the Science and Recommendations for Using Wearable Technology in Sleep and Circadian Research is measurement-context evidence for wearable/actigraphy endpoint interpretation.
implication: Use this source to frame sleep-onset, sleep-efficiency, WASO, duration, or sleep-stage outputs as noisy measurement signals; it does not support a direct efficacy claim for red-light glasses before bed.
caveat: Recommendation/review source; not a direct red-light-glasses trial.

headline: World Sleep Society Recommendations for the Use of Wearable Consumer Health Trackers That Monitor Sleep is measurement-context evidence for wearable/actigraphy endpoint interpretation.
implication: Use this source to frame sleep-onset, sleep-efficiency, WASO, duration, or sleep-stage outputs as noisy measurement signals; it does not support a direct efficacy claim for red-light glasses before bed.
caveat: General recommendations; not specific to red-light glasses or any one device.

headline: A Performance Validation of Six Commercial Wrist-Worn Wearable Sleep-Tracking Devices for Sleep Stage Scoring Compared to Polysomnography is measurement-context evidence for wearable/actigraphy endpoint interpretation.
implication: Use this source to frame sleep-onset, sleep-efficiency, WASO, duration, or sleep-stage outputs as noisy measurement signals; it does not support a direct efficacy claim for red-light glasses before bed.
caveat: Device- and firmware-specific validation; not direct protocol efficacy evidence.

headline: Broad spectacle-lens review limits eye-strain, sleep, and macular-health claims
implication: The protocol page can cite this source for conservative claim boundaries and adverse-event tracking, not for a direct bedtime red-glasses efficacy claim.
caveat: The intervention class is broader than red/amber bedtime eyewear and many included outcomes are short-term or subjective.

headline: Pregnancy RCT found earlier melatonin onset with blue-blocking glasses, but population and control lens limit transfer.
implication: Supports a melatonin mechanism under special conditions, not direct general sleep efficacy.
caveat: Third-trimester pregnancy and partial blue-blocker comparator.

headline: Timed blue light plus morning blue blockers did not improve circadian adaptation in fast rotating shift workers.
implication: Avoid assuming blue-blocking timing always improves circadian outcomes.
caveat: Shift-work combined intervention and different circadian goal.

headline: Blue-blocking glasses showed mania-treatment signals in a small supervised RCT.
implication: Supports psychiatric boundary language for virtual darkness rather than consumer sleep claims.
caveat: Clinical inpatient mania add-on treatment with small analysis sample.

headline: Objective actigraphy meta-analysis found no statistically significant pooled benefit.
implication: Protocol pages should avoid universal objective sleep claims and should distinguish subjective from wearable endpoints.
caveat: Only three small crossover RCTs were eligible.

headline: CIE S 026 supplies the α-opic/melanopic measurement basis for lens and light-dose claims.
implication: Supports using melanopic or α-opic dose terms when evaluating glasses, room light, and screens.
caveat: Measurement standard, not protocol efficacy evidence.

headline: Larger mania RCT did not find blue-blocking glasses superior to lightly tinted control lenses.
implication: Preserves negative clinical evidence and prevents overstating virtual-darkness claims.
caveat: Acute psychiatric inpatient population; not a consumer sleep study.

headline: Pregnancy RCT found no significant blue-blocker advantage on sleep outcomes versus partial blockers.
implication: Adds a population-specific null sleep-outcome boundary and safety notes.
caveat: Control lenses partially blocked blue light; population was healthy pregnant women.

headline: Healthy-adult trial did not find objective sleep benefit.
implication: Protocol expectations should be lower for already-healthy sleepers and should emphasize individual response tracking.
caveat: Some subgroup/self-report signals appeared, but overall objective outcomes did not improve.

headline: Consensus light guidance supports bright days, dim evenings, and darkness during sleep.
implication: Frames glasses as one possible tool for meeting an evening melanopic-light target without encouraging all-day blue-light avoidance.
caveat: Consensus dose guidance, not a red-light-glasses clinical trial.

headline: AAO guidance is an eye-health claim boundary, not bedtime-eyewear efficacy evidence
implication: The protocol should not imply retinal-protection or digital-eye-strain treatment benefits from bedtime red glasses.
caveat: Professional guidance should be checked against the live page before release because public pages can be updated.

headline: College of Optometrists guidance argues against broad blue-blocking lens claims
implication: Protocol language should avoid generic blue-blocker marketing claims and keep any sleep hypothesis tied to evening light reduction.
caveat: The position is broader than red/amber bedtime eyewear and does not provide source-owned bedtime trial effects.

headline: AOP position statement separates eye-health claims from circadian context
implication: Use it to avoid overclaiming eye-health benefits while allowing that evening light exposure may be relevant to sleep timing.
caveat: This is a professional guidance source and does not test red glasses before bed.

headline: Updated review keeps visual, retinal, and sleep claims inconclusive
implication: Use as a current claim-boundary source and note that red/amber lens directness is limited by review inclusion rules.
caveat: Narrative review and excludes some broad-spectrum red/amber filters.

headline: Blue-light shield eyewear preserved melatonin and improved sleep initiation metrics in a small device-use trial.
implication: Supports a mechanistic direct claim that high-filtering evening glasses may help when pre-bed screen/device light is present.
caveat: Small sample and short-communication detail; not a long-term or broad-population trial.

headline: Melanopsin-era light work needs photoreceptor-specific reporting, not photopic lux alone.
implication: Supports using melanopic or spectral measures when evaluating room light, screens, and glasses.
caveat: Methods review, not an efficacy trial.

headline: Large screen-time RCT does not confirm eye-strain benefit
implication: Do not use eye-strain relief as a core claim for red glasses before bed.
caveat: The setting was screen-time exposure, not a bedtime circadian protocol.

headline: Amber lenses improved subjective sleep quality and positive affect in a small adult trial.
implication: Supports a subjective sleep-quality self-experiment signal.
caveat: No objective sleep or circadian baseline measures were extracted.

headline: Lens class and light source jointly determine circadian-relevant transmission.
implication: Supports specifying lens/product class and evening light environment instead of generic blue-blocker use.
caveat: Bench measurement source without user outcomes, fit, or adherence data.

headline: Commercial blue-blocking lenses showed wide variation in modeled circadian and visual effects.
implication: Supports product-quality and safety guardrails rather than generic blue-blocking recommendations.
caveat: Optical modelling source; no sleep or adverse-event outcomes.

headline: Some commercial blue-blocking lenses may still transmit circadian-relevant blue light.
implication: Supports screening lens adequacy before treating eyewear as a valid evening-light intervention.
caveat: Modelled optical/circadian effect, not direct sleep-outcome evidence.

headline: Athlete pilot found subjective benefits but no significant actigraphy differences.
implication: Use as direct evidence for subjective endpoints and as a boundary for wearable claims.
caveat: Short pilot in recreational athletes.

headline: Several marketed blue-light blockers may miss LED wavelengths relevant to evening-light reduction.
implication: Supports requiring spectral/fidelity guardrails before treating a product as suitable for the bedtime protocol.
caveat: Bench optical study; no sleep, melatonin, or adherence outcomes.

headline: Yellow lenses did not improve simulated night pedestrian detection
implication: The bedtime protocol should not imply tinted lenses improve nighttime visibility; users should prioritize safe movement in dim rooms.
caveat: Yellow night-driving glasses are adjacent, not the same as red glasses used while stationary before bed.

headline: HEV-filtering spectacle lenses may transmit substantial blue/cyan light.
implication: Supports separating mild HEV-filtering products from strong pre-bed circadian-light filters.
caveat: Bench lens-transmission study without biological outcomes.

headline: Blue-light-blocking coatings reduced but did not eliminate short-wavelength transmission.
implication: Supports caution that coating-only products may be inadequate for bedtime circadian-light reduction.
caveat: Short optical measurement report, not a sleep or melatonin study.

headline: Blue-blocking lenses can reduce blue colour contrast sensitivity
implication: Protocol safety language should acknowledge possible color/contrast visibility tradeoffs.
caveat: This is an acute visual-performance result, not a sleep outcome.

headline: Blue-light filtering lenses can alter speed perception
implication: Protocol guidance should discourage visually demanding tasks while wearing strong red/blue-blocking lenses.
caveat: The tested lens types and task are not the same as bedtime sleep use.

headline: Student feasibility study showed high adherence and no reported adverse events, with preliminary efficacy signals.
implication: Supports feasibility and safety framing for a home protocol, but not definitive efficacy.
caveat: Small feasibility design was not powered for efficacy.

headline: Orange blue-blocker lenses prevented bright-light melatonin suppression in an acute nighttime study.
implication: Mechanistically supports requiring high-filtering amber/red lenses rather than weak clear computer lenses.
caveat: Acute laboratory melatonin-suppression study, not a home sleep-outcome trial.

headline: Blue-blocking filters did not clearly reduce digital eye-strain symptoms
implication: Avoid using digital-eye-strain relief as a promised benefit of bedtime red glasses.
caveat: The intervention was a filter during a task, not red glasses before bed.

headline: Blue-blocking filters did not alleviate signs or symptoms of digital eye strain
implication: Keep eye-strain relief out of core protocol claims.
caveat: Screen filters are not red bedtime glasses and the task exposure was short.

headline: Blue-blocking screen filter did not improve visual discomfort or accommodation
implication: Avoid translating screen-filter results into promised bedtime eyewear comfort benefits.
caveat: Filter/screen task, not glasses before bed.

headline: Broad systematic review found promising sleep-onset evidence but heterogeneous mood evidence.
implication: Useful for landscape framing and subgroup boundaries, not for a single pooled protocol estimate.
caveat: Heterogeneous designs and populations; includes uncontrolled studies and conference abstracts.

headline: Blue-filtering IOL review does not justify consumer macular-protection claims
implication: The protocol page should not borrow retinal-protection claims from IOL literature.
caveat: Surgical IOL evidence is a major population and modality mismatch.

headline: AMD/pseudophakia filter study highlights low-light visual-performance cautions
implication: The protocol should flag eye disease and low-light mobility as caution zones rather than claiming safety for everyone.
caveat: Special clinical population and acute tasks; not bedtime sleep evidence.

headline: Abstract-only meta-analysis reported mixed objective and subjective effects.
implication: Use only as historical context and do not rely on it over full-text syntheses.
caveat: Abstract-only; participant count missing; one reported CI/p-value combination appears inconsistent.

headline: Tinted lenses can trade contrast gains for color-discrimination losses
implication: Protocol safety language should not assume red lenses are visually neutral.
caveat: Small, older acute study; not a sleep intervention.

headline: Pilot insomnia study linked nocturnal amber lenses to working-memory and sleep improvements.
implication: Adds cognitive-context support but should be counted carefully because it overlaps the insomnia lens trial evidence.
caveat: Small pilot with possible practice effects and no multiple-comparison correction.

headline: IOL retinal-protection evidence has important limitations
implication: Use as an appraisal caution for macular-health claims, not as protocol evidence.
caveat: Commentary/evidence-analysis and a modality mismatch.

headline: Chromatic filters can alter visual performance
implication: Use as background for safety language around color and contrast changes.
caveat: Older acute visual-performance source with no extracted sleep outcome.
